argument: If rights are well defined, information is adequate, bargaining is costless, and agreements are enforceable, affected parties can negotiate an efficient allocation regardless of the initial assignment of rights. Initial rights still determine distribution, and real institutions matter because transaction costs are rarely zero.
boundary: The benchmark assumes negligible search, bargaining, enforcement, and strategic costs.
Many parties, asymmetric information, wealth constraints, and nonconvexities can prevent efficient bargaining.
Efficiency does not imply fairness or political legitimacy.
claim: If rights are well defined, information is adequate, bargaining is costless, and agreements are enforceable, affected parties can negotiate an efficient allocation regardless of the initial assignment of rights. Initial rights still determine distribution, and real institutions matter because transaction costs are rarely zero.
interpretation: The theorem is best treated as a diagnostic benchmark: it directs attention to the concrete transaction costs that make institutions necessary.
